Honourable
ŏn´our-a-ble
adj. (worthy of honour, held in esteem; rendering Hebrew kabed, nikbad, Greek entimos, timios)
From Latin honorabilis, from honor. The Hebrew is kabed, heavy — an honourable man is a man of weight, whose word carries.

Biblical Definition

Honourable in Scripture means weighty, and the Hebrew idiom makes the metaphor plain: to honour is to make heavy, and to despise is to make light. Ahimelech commends David to Saul in these terms: “who is so faithful among all thy servants as David… and is honourable in thine house?” (1Sa 22:14). Samuel is introduced to Saul's servant as “an honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass” (1Sa 9:6) — honour resting on the reliability of his word, which is the truest ground of it. David's mighty men are ranked by it: “He was more honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the first three” (2Sa 23:23). And the most instructive use is Naaman: “a great man with his master, and honourable… he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” (2Ki 5:1). Four clauses of honour, and one word that undoes them all. Honour cannot reach what a man most needs cured.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines honourable as worthy of honour, illustrious, noble, and also as conferring honour, or consistent with honour and reputation — and as performed with marks of honour.

expand to see more

HON´ORABLE, a. Holding a distinguished rank in society; illustrious or noble.

2. Possessing a high mind; actuated by principles of honor, or a nice sense of right and wrong.

3. Conferring honor.

4. Consistent with honor or reputation. 5. Honored; esteemed; regarded with respect.

Key Scripture

2Ki 5:1 — "Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper."

1Sa 9:6 — "And he said unto him, Behold now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is an honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass: now let us go thither; peradventure he can shew us our way that we should go."

1Sa 22:14 — "Then Ahimelech answered the king, and said, And who is so faithful among all thy servants as David, which is the king's son in law, and goeth at thy bidding, and is honourable in thine house?"

2Sa 23:23 — "He was more honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the first three. And David set him over his guard."

Modern Corruption

Reputation mistaken for honour — standing managed and purchased rather than earned by a word that holds — while the one thing a man most needs cured goes unaddressed behind it.

expand to see more

2 Kings 5:1 is one of the most efficient sentences in Scripture. Naaman is great, honourable, victorious, a mighty man in valour — and then five words: but he was a leper. Every honour he holds is genuine and none of it reaches the thing that will kill him, and the cure comes through a captive Israelite servant girl and a prophet who does not come outside to meet him. The whole narrative is an assault on honour as a category of self-assessment, and Naaman's rage at being told to wash in Jordan is precisely the rage of an honourable man asked to be treated like anyone else.

1 Samuel 9:6 supplies the positive ground the age has lost. Samuel is honourable because all that he saith cometh surely to pass — honour resting on a word that holds. Where reputation is a managed asset, built by presentation and defended by publicists, the connection between honour and reliability is severed, and the word becomes a description of standing rather than of substance. Recovering the Hebrew sense would settle much: an honourable man is one whose word is heavy enough to build on.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kabed (H3513), to be heavy, and so to be honoured — the same root as glory; nikbad, the honoured or weighty one; Greek entimos (G1784), held in honour, precious.

expand to see more

Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, honoured; the fifth commandment's honour thy father is literally make heavy.

Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, and hence to curse or despise; the exact antonym, so that contempt is making light of a person.

Greek entimos (G1784) — held in honour, precious; used of the centurion's servant (Luk 7:2) and of the chief corner stone (1Pe 2:6).

Usage

"“A great man… and honourable… but he was a leper” — four honours, undone by one word."

"“An honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass” — honour resting on a reliable word."

"“More honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the first three”."
